value.overview: The Yellow-crowned Night Heron is a medium-sized wading bird of the Americas, named for the yellow crown and long yellow plumes of the adult. It is strongly associated with coastal wetlands but also uses freshwater habitats inland. Unlike many herons, it specializes in crabs, crayfish, and other aquatic invertebrates. It is most active at dusk and during the night, although individuals may forage in daylight when tides or food availability make this advantageous.
value.classification: The Yellow-crowned Night Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the order Pelecaniformes. Its scientific name is Nyctanassa violacea.
value.identification: Adults have a slate-gray to purplish body, a bold black-and-white head pattern, a thick dark bill, and a yellow crown with long pale plumes. The legs are yellowish. Juveniles are brown, heavily streaked and spotted, and can resemble juvenile Black-crowned Night Herons. Yellow-crowned juveniles usually have a heavier bill, longer-looking legs and neck, and fewer, smaller pale spots on the wings. In flight, the legs extend beyond the tail.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from the southeastern United States through Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America. In Costa Rica it is recorded on both the Caribbean and Pacific lowlands, mainly below about 500 meters, although occasional individuals have been found at higher elevations. It uses mangroves, tidal creeks, mudflats, lagoons, marshes, river margins, ponds, and wet forest edges. Mangroves and gallery forests are especially important for roosting.
value.migrationStatus: Resident and migratory populations both occur in Costa Rica. The species is present year-round in suitable lowland wetlands, while some individuals—especially from northern populations—move south during the nonbreeding season. Costa Rican records are generally more frequent along the coasts and in lowland wetland habitats.
value.breeding: Yellow-crowned Night Herons usually nest in trees or shrubs near water, including mangrove stands, wooded swamps, and other wetland forests. They may nest in colonies with other herons or as isolated pairs. The nest is a platform of sticks, and both adults help incubate the eggs and feed the young. Nesting activity and local breeding status in Costa Rica are less thoroughly documented than in the northern part of the species’ range, so regional timing can vary with rainfall and habitat conditions.
value.dietFeeding: Crabs and crayfish are the principal foods in many parts of its range. The species also takes other crustaceans, aquatic insects, fish, frogs, small reptiles, and other small aquatic animals. It usually forages by standing still or walking slowly through shallow water, mudflats, marsh vegetation, or along mangrove edges. Prey is seized with a quick lunge and may be shaken, dismembered, or swallowed whole.
value.behavior: This heron often rests quietly in trees or dense vegetation during the day and becomes more conspicuous at dusk or after dark. It is mainly crepuscular and nocturnal but may feed by day, especially around changing tides. Individuals commonly forage alone and maintain a deliberate, hunched posture while stalking prey. Its flight is steady, with the neck retracted and the long legs projecting beyond the tail.

conservation.populationTrend: The species is widespread and globally secure, although available assessments indicate a slight overall decline, probably linked to habitat loss and degradation.
conservation.threats: Loss, degradation, and disturbance of coastal wetlands, mangroves, marshes, and nesting habitat can reduce feeding and breeding opportunities. Human disturbance near roosts and colonies may also affect nesting success.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore mangroves, marshes, lagoons, and other shallow wetlands. Keep a respectful distance from roosting and nesting birds, avoid disturbing colonies, support wetland conservation, and report sightings through reputable bird-monitoring programs.
